messages.subject: Re: convergence problem(R_hat > 1.1)
messages.body_plain:
Hello bstat,

A few thoughts here:

 - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be
simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
 that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.

 - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might
also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.

 - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information

 - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
 For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.

 - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
the MCMC where it left off.

A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing
the data though we understand that might be confidential).

Chris

messages.subject: MCAR under development on Nimble
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Chris for the previous advice about the matrix handling

I have developed the following MCAR code for 3 disease model on Nimble.
It involved a call to a R function set up as kron for kronecker product
and tries to fit an MCAR with PCAR components using LMC

CM2<-as.carCM(adj[1:L],weights[1:L],num[1:Nareas])
C<-CM2$C
M<-CM2$M
 bou<-carBounds(C,adj,num,M)
if(bou[1]<0)bou[1]=0
 R = structure(.Data = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), .Dim = c(3,3))
Q = structure(.Data = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), .Dim = c(3,3))
 K<-Ndiseases
###################################################################
kl<-K*Nareas
mumod<-rep(0,length=Nareas)
LSTConsts<-list(C,M,bou,Nareas,Ndiseases,mumod,E,num,adj,sumNumNeigh,L,R,K,kl)

 names(LSTConsts)=c('C','M','bou','Nareas','Ndiseases','mumod','E','num','adj','sumNumNeigh','L','R','K','kl')
kron <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(2), y = double(2)){}, Rfun = 'kronecker',
+                     returnType = double(2), envir = .GlobalEnv)
ustar<-matrix(0,nrow=kl,ncol=1)
phistar<-matrix(0,nrow=kl,ncol=1)
The code is here:

MCRcode<-nimbleCode(
+ {
+ for (i in 1:Nareas)
+ {
+ for (k in 1:Ndiseases)
+ {O[i,k]~dpois(mu[i,k])
+        log(mu[i,k])<-log(E[i,k])+log(theta[i,k])
+ log(theta[i,k])<-a0[k]+phi[i,k]+v[i,k]
+ v[i,k]~dnorm(0,tauv[k])}
+ }
+ for (k in 1:Ndiseases){
+ a0[k]~dnorm(0,tau0[k])
+ tauv[k]<-1/pow(sdv[k],2)
+ sdv[k]~dunif(0,10)
+ tau0[k]<-1/pow(sd0[k],2)
+ sd0[k]~dunif(0,10)
+ tauu[k]<-1/pow(sdu[k],2)
+ sdu[k]~dunif(0,10)
+ gamma[k]~dunif(bou[1],bou[2])
+ u[1:Nareas,k]~dcar_proper(mumod[1:Nareas],C[1:L],adj[1:L],num[1:Nareas],M[1:Nareas],tauu[k],gamma[k])
+ }
+ Prec[1:K,1:K]~dwish(R[1:K,1:K],K)
+ Cov[1:K,1:K]<-inverse(Prec[1:K,1:K])
+ Achol[1:K,1:K]<-chol(Cov[1:K,1:K])
+ #IndM<-identityMatrix(Nareas)
+ asd[1:kl,1:kl]<-kron(Achol[1:K,1:K],identityMatrix(Nareas))
+
+ for(i in 1:Nareas){
+ for(k in 1:K){
+ ustar[k+K*(i-1),1]<-u[i,k]
+ }}
+ #phistar[1:kl,1]<-ustar[1:kl,1]
+ phistar[1:kl,1]<-asd[1:kl,1:kl]%*%ustar[1:kl,1]
+ for(i in 1:Nareas){
+ for(k in 1: K){
+ phi[i,k]<-phistar[k+K*(i-1),1]}}
+ })
>
> LSTinits<-list(a0=c(-0.1,-0.1,-0.1),0.1,sdv=c(0.1,0.1,0.1),sdu=0.1,
+ sd0=c(0.1,0.1,0.1),gamma=c(0.5,0.5,0.5),sdu=c(0.1,0.1,0.1),
+ u=structure(.Data=rep(0,477),.Dim=c(159,3)),
+ v=structure(.Data=rep(0,477),.Dim=c(159,3)),
+ Prec=structure(.Data=c(5.3, 0,0, 0, 4.1,0,0,0,2.3),.Dim=c(3,3)))
> #####################################################################
>  LST<-nimbleModel(code=MCRcode,name="LST",constants=LSTConsts,
+ data=LSTdata,inits=LSTinits)

when nimbleMCMC is called it gives an error when it tries to run the chin:

> #####################################################################
> LST2<-nimbleMCMC(code=MCRcode,constants=LSTConsts,data=LSTdata,inits=LSTinits,niter=5000,nburnin=3000)
defining model...
Adding C, M, mumod, num, adj, R as data for building model.
building model...
setting data and initial values...
running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...
checking model sizes and dimensions...
checking model calculations...
model building finished.
compiling... this may take a minute. Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
compilation finished.
running chain 1...
Error: attempt to use zero-length variable name

Any advice welcome!
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: NIMBLE freezes using dcar_proper model
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dr.Turek

I have a similar but slightly different problem when using rcar_proper to generate car random effects.  My simulation is just a 10 by 10 square lattice grids then I feed my adjacent matrix and num into rcar_proper function, a warning showed up that 'eves' have imaginary parts. I adopted your suggestion to use R's eigen() function, and 'eves' still have imaginary parts with extremely small values.
Does it matter to feed only the 'real' part of 'eves' to rcar_proper  since the imaginary parts are pretty small and omittable?  Then are the random spatial effects obtained trustable? I notice the example you used in the manual actually has a  one-dimensional structure rather than two dimensions, that structure works but a square structure with more than 3 by 3 has the problem. Thanks very much.

在 2019年4月11日星期四 UTC-5下午2:17:13，Daniel Turek写道：

> Dan, thanks for posting your question, and also for following up separately, off-list, to share your model and data set so we could diagnose the problem you're experiencing.
>
> As it turns out, the underlying library we use for matrix algebra (the Eigen C++ package) appears to *not* handle your particular spatial adjacency structure very well.  Specifically, when the NIMBLE model object is constructed, under-the-hood NIMBLE reparameterizes your model to our "canonical" parameterization, which has the advantage of pre-calculating some fixed constants (based up the spatial adjacency structure), which will then be immediately available for use during the course of MCMC sampling (and will never need to be re-calculated again).  The canonical parameterization for the CAR proper distribution is takes the form:
>
> s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu, C, adj, num, M, tau, gamma, evs)
>
> where "C", "M", and "evs" are deterministically calculated from the "adj" and "num" vectors.
>
> The specific problem comes from generating "evs", which is the vector of N eigenvalues of an intermediate NxN matrix.  It's during that eigen decomposition of this matrix, being done by the Eigen C++ library, that appears to scale very poorly for your particular adjacency structure, and appears to "hang", as it never seems to finish the computation.
>
> I have two alternate paths forward for you, either of which should work:
>
> Option 1. Oddly, R's native eigen() decomposition functionality appears to work fine for your model.  So, getting around this problem is as easy as doing these pre-calculations yourself in R (which will use R's eigen() function, which appears to work fine for your spatial structure), then parameterizing your proper CAR distribution as shown above, and additionally providing the (pre-calculated) "C", "M", and "evs" values through the "constants" list for creating your model.  Thus, your modified code would look something like:
>
> C <- nimble::CAR_calcC(adj, num)
> M <- nimble::CAR_calcM(num)
> Cmatrix <- nimble::CAR_calcCmatrix(C, adj, num)
> evs <- eigen(Cmatrix, only.values = TRUE)$values    ## using R's eigen()
>
> ## old constants list:
> ##constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N)
>
> ## new constants list:
> constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N, C=C, M=M, evs=evs)
>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>     ...
>     ## new dcar_proper parametization:
>     s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu[1:N], C=C[1:L], adj=adj[1:L], num=num[1:N], M=M[1:N], tau=tau, gamma=gamma, evs=evs[1:N])
>     ...
> })
>
> ## define "data", and "inits", the same as you already are
>
> Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
>
> This construction of the model, already having pre-calculated "evs" yourself in R, should work fine, and can be carried through to building an MCMC, compilation, and running the compiled MCMC.
>
> Option 2: It also appears to be the case that the Eigen C++ library is able to handle the eigen decomposition fine, if we only request the eigen *values* (since that's all we need), and not the eigen *vectors*.  So, I've made this change to the underlying NIMBLE code for the proper CAR distribution, to only calculate the eigen *values*.  Using this approach, it finishes in a reasonably short time.  I've made these changes, and pushed them to the development branch of nimble ("devel"), which you can install using:
>
> remove.packages('nimble')
> library(devtools)
> install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
> library(nimble)
>
> Once you have the updated package installed, your original code that you were using should work fine.  (And give, literally, identical calculations and inferences to Option 1 above).  So, it's up to you if you want to install this updated version of nimble, or to re-parameterize your model slightly.  Also, this change in the development branch will be included in our next release of the nimble package, whenever that is.
>
> I hope this sorts it out, but please keep in touch with any other questions.
>
> Cheers!
> Daniel
>
>
>
>
>

> On Thu, Apr 11, 2019 at 1:17 PM <drfi...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I appreciate the development of NIMBLE and it is a great tool. I am having some difficulty in running a dcar_proper model with my full dataset.  In my case, NIMBLE freezes after:
> >
> > “running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...”
> >
> >
> > I used the USGS Adjacency For WinBUGS Tool to extract the neighbor adjacency structure for my dataset. My dataset is on a stream network and consists of 86 sites with between 16 and 50+ reaches (~100m in length) at each site. This is referred to as the full dataset and includes all 1628 reaches (pres_num_adj.csv). In the simplest case for a site, there are 8 reaches for fish presence immediately followed by 8 fish absence reaches upstream. I plan to use GIS attributes (gradient, flow, etc.) to model the upper most occurrence of salmon in a stream using CAR models.  Because of this design the autocorrelation is over 95% between adjacent reaches. Not having done this before, I used the CAR examples in the NIMBLE manual to better understand these models and the code.  I followed up with ICAR and CAR proper model using my data with no covariates to develop models and will eventually follow up with covariate models.

> >

The car proper model runs on the “short’ dataset but will not run on the full dataset and freezes after “running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...”

> >
> > I have checked the data structure in the csv files and it seems appropriate. I am using NIMBLE VERSION 0.7.0. I have used the latest R version and 3.4.4.  I have used Rstudio and directly run NIMBLE through the R GUI.  Despite all of this the problem still persist for the full dataset for the CAR proper model.

> > Any suggestions would be appreciated and I would be happy to send you the code and data if that helps.  Thanks for considering this request.

> A few thoughts here:

>  - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be
> simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
> One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
>  that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.
>
>  - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might
> also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.
>
>  - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information
>
>  - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.

>  - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.

Hi Broti,

A couple of issues jump out from your example.  One is that you should use "x[i] ~" instead of "x[i] <-" to make x[i] a stochastic node.  Another is that you have made dmultinorm call rtmvnorm, so you have a "d" function calling an "r" function.  This doesn't make sense.  I think you want dmultinorm to call dtmvnorm.

-Perry

Hi Broti,

A couple of issues jump out from your example.  One is that you should use "x[i] ~" instead of "x[i] <-" to make x[i] a stochastic node.  Another is that you have made dmultinorm call rtmvn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Broti,

It doesn't make sense to use an "r" function in a nimble model.

If one has

x[i] ~ dnorm(mean, sd = sigma),

this is, in effect, converted to

logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)

MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.

One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".

If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then

Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')

will, in effect, be converted to

x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).

In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.

Please try something like
dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),

                                 upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm',

                                 returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

with
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
   for(i in 1:4) {x[i] ~ dmultinorm(mean = 0, sigma = 1, lower = 0, upper = 1)}
})

Also please read the user manual sections on nimbleRcall and on user-defined distributions.  I think those two sections provide the details you need.

On Monday, May 6, 2019 at 1:15:40 PM UTC-4, nimble.stats wrote:

> Hi Broti,
>

>
> If one has

>
> logProb_x[i] <- dnorm(x[i], mean, sigma, log = TRUE)
>
> MCMC needs to calculate "d" functions, not to simulate from "r" functions.
>
> One can simulate with a nimble model.  When one does so, nimble automatically uses the corresponding "r" function based on a name like "dnorm".
>
> If the above declaration for x[i] is in a model, enclosed in for(i in 1:10), then
>
> Rmodel$simulate('x[3]')
>

>
> x[3] <- rnorm(1, mean, sigma).
>
> In both of your trials, the error message says the first argument to a "d" function should be  "x".  This is similar to all R density functions.  E.g. the first argument to dnorm is x.  The immediate problem in both of your trials is that you have made the first argument to both nimbleRcalls be "n".  Normally, "n" is the first argument to an "r" function but not a "d" function.
>

> dmultinorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(), mean = double(), sigma =  double(), lower = integer(0),
>                                  upper = integer(0)){}, Rfun = 'dtmvnorm',

> > > > > Hello bstat,

> > > > > A few thoughts here:

> > > > >  - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be
> > > > > simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
> > > > > One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
> > > > >  that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.
> > > > >
> > > > >  - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might
> > > > > also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.
> > > > >
> > > > >  - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information
> > > > >
> > > > >  - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
> > > > >  For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
> > > > > To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.
> > > > >
> > > > >  - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.
> > > > >
> > > > > There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
> > > > > the MCMC where it left off.

messages.body_plain:
If the arguments to dmultinorm (mean, sigma, lower, upper) need to be non-scalar, they should be declared as such using double(1) or double(2) instead of double() (which defaults to double(0)), where double(nDim) has nDim = number of dimensions.  Please see the user manual chapter on writing nimbleFunctions.  Also, you may need to give index ranges explicitly, such as zero[1:4] instead of zero[].  Please see the user manual sections on writing models.

> > > > > > also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >  - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information
> > > > > >
> > > > > >  - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
> > > > > >  For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
> > > > > > To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >  - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart
> > > > > > the MCMC where it left off.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > A couple other requests - please do include your name when mailing the list and do provide code that will run. Your code is missing dimensions for some of the variables ( as well as not providing

messages.subject: Re: convergence problem(R_hat > 1.1)
messages.body_plain:
You are confusing the length of an object with the number of dimensions.

You have written x = double(4), I think with the idea that that implies length of 4.  As indicated in my previous answer and in the user manual, the type declaration for double gives the *number of dimensions*.  For a vector, this would be 1.  So you would want x = double(1) to indicate that x is 1-dimensional.

> > > > > > > > A few thoughts here:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  - it may be that the (0,1) constraint on the elements of dmnorm-distributed values slows mixing because a large number of constraints must all be
> > > > > > > > simultaneously satisfied. To get a better sense, you might remove the constaints temporarily and see if mixing is much better so you know if that is the cause.
> > > > > > > > One possibility if you wanted to invest some time in this would be to remove the constraint and write your own user-defined sampler (documented in our manual)
> > > > > > > >  that implements the conjugate (i.e. Gibbs) update for beta_X but rejects any proposal that violates the constraint. That might work better than relying on NIMBLE's block samplers.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  - given that the model as written uses NIMBLE's Metropolis random walk block samplers, it's often the case that you need good initial values. You might
> > > > > > > > also want to experiment with changing the initial proposal scale for these block samplers.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  - you might also try the AFSS sampler in place of the block samplers and see if that improves matters. See help(samplers) for more information
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  - if you didn't have Phi_X involved in the prior for mu_beta_X as well as the prior for beta_X, then it should be assigned a conjugate sampler, which might mix better.
> > > > > > > >  For a parameter like mu_beta_X for which there is no replication, you may be best off assigning a fairly non-informative prior independently across the elements.
> > > > > > > > To get the conjugate sampler assigned, you might also have to directly use the precision matrix and avoid inverse(), which should also speed up computation.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  - and ultimately, you may just need to run the chain longer.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > There is no way to assess mixing iteration by iteration. As documented in the manual, you can run the chain for a while, check the output, and then restart

messages.body_plain:
Andrew, thanks for sending me the additional data in a separate email.  There were a few things getting you stuck here:

(1) The stray (unnamed) initial value of 0.1, appearing as the second element in your "LSTinits" initial values list.  It turns out NIMBLE doesn't handle "unnamed" list elements for initial values very well.  I just submitted an issue with the nimble package to improve this.

## second elemeng here, "0.1", should be removed.
LSTinits<-list(a0=c(-0.1,-0.1,-0.1),0.1, ....

(2) Another initial values list issue.  You had two declarations of "sdu" in your "LSTinits" list.  The first was a scalar: "sdu=0.1".
That one does't work, since sdu in the model is a length-3 vector in the model.  This first "scalar" declaration needs to be removed.
The second declaration in the list is correct: "sdu=c(0.1,0.1,0.1)".  That matches the model, as a length-3 vector.

(3) Your use of nimbleRcall() for the R kronecker() function *needs to match the *named* arguments* to R's kronecker.  So, change the lower-case x to X, and the lower-case y to Y, in the nimbleRcall() function declaration:

kron <- nimbleRcall(function(X = double(2), Y = double(2)){}, Rfun = 'kronecker',

                    returnType = double(2), envir = .GlobalEnv)

I think making those fixes should get your model (and MCMC) running fine.

Thanks for using NIMBLE, and submitting your question.

Andrew, thanks for sending me the additional data in a separate email.  There were a few things getting you stuck here:

(1) The stray (unnamed) initial value of 0.1, appearing as the second element in your "LSTinits" initial values list.  It turns out NIMBLE doesn't handle "unnamed" list elements for initial values very well.  I just submitted an issue with the nimble package to improve this.

## second elemeng here, "0.1", should be removed.

LSTinits<-list(a0=c(-0.1,-0.1,-0.1),0.1, ....

(2) Another initial values list issue.  You had two declarations of "sdu" in your "LSTinits" list.  The first was a scalar: "sdu=0.1".

That one does't work, since sdu in the model is a length-3 vector in the model.  This first "scalar" declaration needs to be removed.

The second declaration in the list is correct: "sdu=c(0.1,0.1,0.1)".  That matches the model, as a length-3 vector.

(3) Your use of nimbleRcall() for the R kronecker() function *needs to match the *named* arguments* to R's kronecker.  So, change the lower-case x to X, and the lower-case y to Y, in the nimbleRcall() function declaration:

kron <- nimbleRcall(function(X = double(2), Y = double(2)){}, Rfun = 'kronecker',

                    returnType = double(2), envir = .GlobalEnv)

I think making those fixes should get your model (and MCMC) running fine.

Thanks for using NIMBLE, and submitting your question.

I'm looking at a fairly simple CAR model dealing with air pollution.  I've tried to implement a spatially correlated error term by using the dcar_normal distribution from  nimble.  However, whenever I use this distribution, I get many warnings when compiling the model that look like this:

warning: value of deterministic node mu[186, 57]: value is NA or NaN even after trying to calculate.

My model code is:

Mod.Univariate<-nimbleCode({
  for (j in 1:J){
    for(i in 1:I){

      y[i,j] ~ dpois(lambda=mu[i,j])

      log(mu[i,j]) <- a0 + a1*pols.std[i,j] + eps[i] +  e[i]

      #######################################
      #### Add in Demographic Vars Here #####
      #######################################

    }

  }

  for(i in 1:I){
    e[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=sd.e)
  }

  eps[1:I] ~ dcar_normal(adj=adj[1:N], num=num[1:I], tau=tau.eps, zero_mean = 1)

  a1 ~ dnorm(0, sd=sd)
  sd ~ dunif(min=0.01,max=5)

  sd.e ~ dunif(min=0.01,max=5)

  tau.eps ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

  a0 ~ dnorm(0, sd=sd0)
  sd0 ~ dunif(min=0.01,max=5)
})

I've tried several starting values for tau, priors for tau, and configured zero_mean to be both 0 and 1.

adj is of length sum(num) and num is length I (the same length as the vector eps).  I've included the weights as constants (all = 1), included them as being assigned in the model code, and I've left them out entirely, as nimble says it defaults them to all equal 1.  The problem persists regardless of which way I have entered it thus far.  I'm unsure what the issue could be, but it is very possible it is a simple coding error.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.  My full code is included below (note that I am cycling through several model versions and several pollutants -- I have only tried this on version[1] and pollutant[1], but there should be no appreciable difference between these settings, just the values of pols.std):

messages.body_plain:
Raymond, I'm happy to say that I think the problem was as simple as providing names for your initial values.  You code contained the following line to define the initial values list:

nimble.inits <- list(sd=sd, sd.e=sd.e, sd0=sd0, a1=a1, e=e, a0=a0, eps, tau.eps)

The last two elements in this list (eps, tau.eps) are *not provided as named list elements*.  Therefore, when this list is passed into the nimbleModel() function, those final two list elements are merely numerical list elements, without an associated "name", thus nimbleModel() has no way of knowing what model variable(s) they're being supplied for.  As a result, the dcar_normal() distribution was missing values both for the "tau" parameter, and for the spatially correlated errors themselves, for which the MCMC is unable to simulate into.

Anyway, the simple fix is to name these list elements, as:

nimble.inits <- list(sd=sd, sd.e=sd.e, sd0=sd0, a1=a1, e=e, a0=a0, eps=eps, tau.eps=tau.eps)

Then I think you're good to go.  Please let us know how this works for you.

Cheers,
Daniel

On Friday, May 17, 2019 at 9:55:28 AM UTC-4, Daniel Turek wrote:

> Raymond, I'm happy to say that I think the problem was as simple as providing names for your initial values.  You code contained the following line to define the initial values list:
>
> nimble.inits <- list(sd=sd, sd.e=sd.e, sd0=sd0, a1=a1, e=e, a0=a0, eps, tau.eps)
>
> The last two elements in this list (eps, tau.eps) are *not provided as named list elements*.  Therefore, when this list is passed into the nimbleModel() function, those final two list elements are merely numerical list elements, without an associated "name", thus nimbleModel() has no way of knowing what model variable(s) they're being supplied for.  As a result, the dcar_normal() distribution was missing values both for the "tau" parameter, and for the spatially correlated errors themselves, for which the MCMC is unable to simulate into.
>
> Anyway, the simple fix is to name these list elements, as:
>
> nimble.inits <- list(sd=sd, sd.e=sd.e, sd0=sd0, a1=a1, e=e, a0=a0, eps=eps, tau.eps=tau.eps)
>
> Then I think you're good to go.  Please let us know how this works for you.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>

Daniel,

Sorry for the very delayed response.  Thanks very much for the clear answer and for posting solutions.  I used option 2 and this resolved the problem. Thanks again.

On Thursday, April 11, 2019 at 12:17:13 PM UTC-7, Daniel Turek wrote:

> Dan, thanks for posting your question, and also for following up separately, off-list, to share your model and data set so we could diagnose the problem you're experiencing.
>
> As it turns out, the underlying library we use for matrix algebra (the Eigen C++ package) appears to *not* handle your particular spatial adjacency structure very well.  Specifically, when the NIMBLE model object is constructed, under-the-hood NIMBLE reparameterizes your model to our "canonical" parameterization, which has the advantage of pre-calculating some fixed constants (based up the spatial adjacency structure), which will then be immediately available for use during the course of MCMC sampling (and will never need to be re-calculated again).  The canonical parameterization for the CAR proper distribution is takes the form:
>
> s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu, C, adj, num, M, tau, gamma, evs)
>
> where "C", "M", and "evs" are deterministically calculated from the "adj" and "num" vectors.
>
> The specific problem comes from generating "evs", which is the vector of N eigenvalues of an intermediate NxN matrix.  It's during that eigen decomposition of this matrix, being done by the Eigen C++ library, that appears to scale very poorly for your particular adjacency structure, and appears to "hang", as it never seems to finish the computation.
>
> I have two alternate paths forward for you, either of which should work:
>
> Option 1. Oddly, R's native eigen() decomposition functionality appears to work fine for your model.  So, getting around this problem is as easy as doing these pre-calculations yourself in R (which will use R's eigen() function, which appears to work fine for your spatial structure), then parameterizing your proper CAR distribution as shown above, and additionally providing the (pre-calculated) "C", "M", and "evs" values through the "constants" list for creating your model.  Thus, your modified code would look something like:
>
> C <- nimble::CAR_calcC(adj, num)
> M <- nimble::CAR_calcM(num)
> Cmatrix <- nimble::CAR_calcCmatrix(C, adj, num)
> evs <- eigen(Cmatrix, only.values = TRUE)$values    ## using R's eigen()
>
> ## old constants list:
> ##constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N)
>
> ## new constants list:
> constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N, C=C, M=M, evs=evs)
>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>     ...
>     ## new dcar_proper parametization:
>     s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu[1:N], C=C[1:L], adj=adj[1:L], num=num[1:N], M=M[1:N], tau=tau, gamma=gamma, evs=evs[1:N])
>     ...
> })
>
> ## define "data", and "inits", the same as you already are
>
> Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
>
> This construction of the model, already having pre-calculated "evs" yourself in R, should work fine, and can be carried through to building an MCMC, compilation, and running the compiled MCMC.
>
> Option 2: It also appears to be the case that the Eigen C++ library is able to handle the eigen decomposition fine, if we only request the eigen *values* (since that's all we need), and not the eigen *vectors*.  So, I've made this change to the underlying NIMBLE code for the proper CAR distribution, to only calculate the eigen *values*.  Using this approach, it finishes in a reasonably short time.  I've made these changes, and pushed them to the development branch of nimble ("devel"), which you can install using:
>
> remove.packages('nimble')
> library(devtools)
> install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
> library(nimble)
>
> Once you have the updated package installed, your original code that you were using should work fine.  (And give, literally, identical calculations and inferences to Option 1 above).  So, it's up to you if you want to install this updated version of nimble, or to re-parameterize your model slightly.  Also, this change in the development branch will be included in our next release of the nimble package, whenever that is.
>
> I hope this sorts it out, but please keep in touch with any other questions.
>
> Cheers!
> Daniel
>
>

messages.subject: subscript out of bounds error
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit a hierarchical distance sampling model that uses time to detection to estimate availability/temporary emigration, similar to the one in Advanced Hierarchical Modeling (9.3.2, p. 474). The AHM example  <https://github.com/nimble-dev/AHMnimble/blob/master/Chapter_9/Section_9p3p2_example_nimble.R>runs fine in Nimble, and I can run my model in JAGS, but for some reason when I run the buildMCMC function in Nimble I get the error:

Error in expr[[3]] : subscript out of bounds

and I'm not sure what this error is referring to. When I remove N[k] ~ dbin(pavail[k], M[k]) and modify y[k] ~ dbin(pdet[k], M[k]) (ie, just a hierarchical distance sampling model), the model runs fine, so I believe the error is related to the time-removal part of the model. My best guess is it could be something to do with initial values. Also, I get the same error when I run nimbleModelname$checkConjugacy().

I am using nimble package version 0.7.1 in R version 3.5.2 on Windows. I am happy to send a reproducible example off-list.

Thank you for your time,
Adrian

messages.subject: Re: subscript out of bounds error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

Thanks for your off-list reproducible example.

This error is caused by a bug in our conjugacy detection system that was introduced when we modified to system for version 0.7.1 to handle more complicated conjugacies.
We'll fix the bug in version 0.8.0 of NIMBLE, expected to be released in the next couple weeks. But in the interim, please install the patched version of nimble, in one of the two following ways:
a) download and install www.stat.berkeley.edu/~paciorek/transfer/nimble_fix_890/nimble_0.8.0.tar.gz <http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~paciorek/transfer/nimble_fix_890/nimble_0.8.0.tar.gz> (it's a source package rather than the usual Windows binary format, so if you have trouble installing, please let me know and I can give more detailed instructions) or
b) install from Github, from https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble from branch "fix_sum_conj"

Also, a side (but important) note - the mean of your Poisson distribution has negative values in it because you are using the identity link. That may
not be what you want and even if you do, you certainly want to change the initial values so all values of lambda are positive.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ray,

It turned out that you stumbled into a model-specific problem in the configureMCMC step that was accidentally introduced in a relatively recent release.  This is not what I expected to find.

I've pushed a fix to our devel branch.  You can install by

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

Thanks for your patience on this one.

I think you'll find it faster to work outside of nimbleMCMC to save some steps that you don't need:

m <- nimbleModel(Mod.2.0.8, constants = nimble.constants, data = nimble.data, inits = nimble.inits,
                 calculate = FALSE) ## calculate=FALSE is faster

conf <- configureMCMC(m, useConjugacy = FALSE) ## useConjugacy = FALSE is faster, if you don't need Gibbs (conjugate) sampling

Then use buildMCMC and runMCMC.

We're working towards releasing version 0.8.0 soon.  I think that will have efficiency improvements to configureMCMC, but you will have to turn them on via a nimbleOption to try them.  We'll make it clear in release notes.

-Perry

Hi Lokesh,

I'm following up on your case of using nimbleRcall to call dcomp.  I'm glad the workaround of coding dcomp as a nimbleFunction worked.  I tracked down why the nimbleRcall didn't work and have fixed it on our devel branch.   If you need it, you can install by:

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

It will be included in version 0.8.0, which we are working to release soon.

The issue with the nimbleRcall involved management of R's random number generator (RNG).  R provides a system for C code to obtain the RNG seed, use RNG calls as needed, and then put the RNG seed back into R when done.  Both nimble and Rcpp (via Rcpp::export) automatically do this for all calls into C code.  Unfortunately, the C++ generated for a nimbleRcall neglected to manage the RNG seed properly before and after handing control to R.  Since in your case the R code called by your nimbleRcall went on to call into C compiled via Rcpp (i.e. dcomp), there was incorrect management of the RNG seed.

-Perry

On Fri, Apr 12, 2019 at 11:48 AM Lokesh Arya <lokeshar...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thank you so much pdevalpine.
>
> It finally worked.
>
> On Friday, April 12, 2019 at 11:49:30 PM UTC+5:30, pdevalpine wrote:
> > Hi Lokesh,
> >
> > Thanks for making an example with more informative data, so it's more clear that there is a real sampling problem.
> >
> > I think this is revealing a bug related to nimbleRcall and R's garbage collection, which is creating incorrect values being passed from C++ to R or back.  We have seen a bug related to this previously, which we fixed, but evidently there is more to it.  I think it has to do with use of PROTECT in C++ code for R.
> >
> > What convinces me that something like this is the problem is that I was able to write dcomp purely as a nimbleFunction, so that no nimbleRcall is needed, and now the results look reasonable.  To write it this way, I looked at the CompGLM C++ source code, where I saw that the functions dcomp and Z were both easy to write as nimbleFunctions.
> >

> > calcZ <- nimbleFunction(
> >     run = function(lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double()) {
> >         ## CompGLM C++ source code:
> >         ##         double Z(double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
> >         ##  double sum = 1.0;
> >         ##  double factorial = 1.0;
> >         ##  double lamPower = lam;
> >         ##  for (int i = 1; i <= sumTo; ++i) {

> >         ##  sum += lamPower / pow(factorial, nu);
> >         ##  lamPower *= lam;
> >         ##  }
> >         ##  return sum;
> >         ## }
> >         sum <- 1
> >         factorial <- 1
> >         lamPower <- lam
> >         for(i in 1:sumTo) {
> >             factorial <- factorial * i
> >             sum <- sum + lamPower / pow(factorial, nu)
> >             lamPower <- lamPower * lam
> >         }
> >         return(sum)
> >         returnType(double())
> >     }
> > )
> >
> > dCMP_nf <- nimbleFunction(
> >     ## Normally a dist random variable must be called x, but this is not really the dist function being called, so the name "y" will work
> >     run = function(y = double(), lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double(), log = integer(0, default = 0) ) {
> >         ## C source code from package CompGLM (which is wrapped by another layer that handles log):
> >         ##         double dcomp(int y, double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
> >         ##  if (y < 0) {
> >         ##  return 0.0;
> >         ##  } else {
> >         ##  return pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * Z(lam, nu, sumTo));
> >         ##  }
> >         ## }
> >         returnType(double())
> >         if(y < 0) {
> >             if(log) return(-Inf)
> >             else return(0)
> >         } else {
> >             prob <- pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * calcZ(lam, nu, sumTo))
> >             if(log) return(log(prob))
> >             else return(prob)
> >         }
> >     }
> > )
> >
> > dZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
> >     run = function(x = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
> >         returnType(double())
> > ##        print("x = ", x, " lam = ", lam, " nu = ", nu, " zeroProb = ", zeroProb)

> >         if(x != 0) {

> >             ## or the probability if log = FALSE
> >             else return((1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE))
> >         }
> >         ## From here down we know x is 0
> >         totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(0, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE)
> >         if(log) return(log(totalProbZero))
> >         return(totalProbZero)

messages.subject: Re: Memory Issues
messages.body_plain:
A clarification:  The fix to the problem you encountered will definitely be in 0.8.0.  *Other* efficiency improvements will be available by turning on an option.  They will go in a future release after they've been tested more thoroughly.

On Wed, May 29, 2019 at 3:00 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Ray,
>
> It turned out that you stumbled into a model-specific problem in the configureMCMC step that was accidentally introduced in a relatively recent release.  This is not what I expected to find.
>
> I've pushed a fix to our devel branch.  You can install by
>
> library(devtools)
> install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")
>
> Thanks for your patience on this one.
>
> I think you'll find it faster to work outside of nimbleMCMC to save some steps that you don't need:
>
> m <- nimbleModel(Mod.2.0.8, constants = nimble.constants, data = nimble.data, inits = nimble.inits,
>                  calculate = FALSE) ## calculate=FALSE is faster
>
> conf <- configureMCMC(m, useConjugacy = FALSE) ## useConjugacy = FALSE is faster, if you don't need Gibbs (conjugate) sampling
>
> Then use buildMCMC and runMCMC.
>
> We're working towards releasing version 0.8.0 soon.  I think that will have efficiency improvements to configureMCMC, but you will have to turn them on via a nimbleOption to try them.  We'll make it clear in release notes.
>
> -Perry
>

Hi,

I have been working with a problem with truncated distribution, where Y ~ N(X*B, sigma), B ~ trunc_MN(mu, Omega), Omega ~ IW(psi, P) ans mu~MN(0,I). now if I use constraints for beta [ constraint_X_bound[j,m] ~ dconstraint(0 < beta_X[j,m] & beta_X[j,m] <= 1) ] then nimble is too slow and causing divergence (R_hat > 1.1), so I created my own truncated distribution.

Now my problem is posterior of Omega follows some distribution like IW(a1, b1)/ cdf(B, lower, upper). can anyone please propose how to generate random variable for posterior of omega.

Any help is appreciated.

Thank you.

Hi Luiza,

Thanks for the reproducible example.  I also got an error message, but it was more informative:
Error: Type double of the return() argument does not match type integer given in the returnType() statement (void is default).

I'm not sure if we got different error messages because I am running on our development branch (devel) or not, but, just in case, please be sure you have the current version of nimble.

In any case, try changing "returnType(integer(1))" to "returnType(double(1))".  Although they are integer values, they will be treated as doubles and need to be declared that way.

Also, you may find it numerically advantageous in dBPois to do the main work on a log scale and then exponentiate at the end if log==FALSE.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
hi Broti,

I'm not fully following your code - I guess that B, beta_X and beta are the same?

In any case, without the truncation, NIMBLE should assign a conjugate sampler to Omega. Once you have truncation on the multivariate normal dependence, NIMBLE should assign a RW_wishart sampler. The tricky thing here is of course that an inverse Wishart realization needs to be positive definite, so many standard samplers won't work. The RW_wishart that should be assigned should work correctly in terms of only proposing positive definite realizations, though there is no guarantee the chain will mix well. Please see help(samplers) for more information on that sampler.

Beyond that I don't have any particular suggestions, but if you get any good advice or find something in the literature, you should be able to implement it as a user-defined sampler, as discussed in the NIMBLE manual.

Chris
